claims.claim: Press & Dyson 2012 (PNAS 109(26):10409–10413, published online 2012-05-21/22, issue 2012-06-26) introduced zero-determinant (ZD) strategies: memory-one strategies with which player X can unilaterally enforce a linear relation between her and her opponent's long-run scores, including fixing the opponent's score.
claims.quote: One specialization of ZD strategies allows X to unilaterally set Y's score.
claims.source_title: Press & Dyson, Iterated Prisoner's Dilemma contains strategies that dominate any evolutionary opponent, PNAS
claims.notes: Memory-one (conditions only on last round), infinitely repeated / long-run average payoffs, no errors. Same paper: 'X cannot unilaterally set her own score in IPD.' PNAS doi page returned 403; text read via PMC. Contributed 2012-04-19 (PNAS 'Contributed' track, Dyson NAS member).

claims.claim: Abstract claims an extortionate ZD player can enforce an extortionate linear relation, and that an 'evolutionary' opponent's best response is to accede; 'only a player with a theory of mind about his opponent can do better', in which case the IPD becomes an Ultimatum Game.
claims.quote: Only a player with a theory of mind about his opponent can do better
claims.source_title: Press & Dyson 2012 PNAS (abstract)
claims.notes: Also verbatim from abstract: 'an evolutionary player's best response is to accede to the extortion.' Full abstract not reproduced (tool quote limit); fetch the PMC page to copy it whole. Discussion: 'If Y has a theory of mind, then IPD is simply an ultimatum game'.

claims.claim: Press & Dyson define an 'evolutionary' player narrowly: one who adjusts his own strategy to improve his score but does not explicitly model X's score or strategy. The 'dominates any evolutionary opponent' title therefore refers to a single fixed-strategy X against one adapting Y, not to population evolution.
claims.quote: but does not otherwise explicitly consider X's score or her own strategy
claims.source_title: Press & Dyson 2012 PNAS (Methods/Discussion)
claims.notes: Key to the media overstatement: 'evolutionary' here ≠ evolving population. Discussion advice: X 'should go to lunch leaving her fixed strategy mindlessly in place'. The word 'dominate' appears only in the title, not in the Discussion (per fetch).

claims.claim: Press & Dyson give an extortion example with extortion factor χ=3 (standard payoffs T=5,R=3,P=1,S=0): if Y fully cooperates, X scores above the mutual-cooperation value 3 and Y below it.
claims.quote: X’s score is always greater than the mutual cooperation value of 3, and Y’s is always less.
claims.source_title: Press & Dyson 2012 PNAS
claims.notes: Phrase 'enforces an extortion factor 3' verified in text; χ symbol and payoff numbers are rendered as images so not text-verified. My own calculation (not from source): χ=3, Y always cooperates → s_X≈3.73, s_Y≈1.91 (s_X−P = 3(s_Y−P)). Verify against PDF before printing numbers.

claims.claim: Press & Dyson explicitly identify Tit-for-Tat as a special (fair) case within the ZD family — the χ=1 / slope-1 boundary of the linear relation s_X−P = χ(s_Y−P), i.e. TFT enforces equal payoffs.
claims.quote: which is the well-known tit-for-tat (TFT) strategy
claims.source_title: Press & Dyson 2012 PNAS
claims.notes: Verbatim phrase confirmed; the fetch reported it arises in 'a special case that implies fairness and at one limit value of a parameter' but the parameter values are images. Also: 'Knowing only TFT among ZD strategies' (verbatim). Hilbe-Nowak-Sigmund 2013 define extortion only for χ>1 and treat TFT separately as (1,0,1,0) — so 'TFT = ZD with χ=1' is accurate as limit/boundary, but TFT is not an 'extortioner'. Check Press–Dyson PDF Eq. for exact parameterization.

claims.claim: Press & Dyson: when both players know about ZD strategies, they may negotiate to set each other's score to the cooperative maximum, and then there is no advantage in defection.
claims.quote: they may choose to negotiate to each set the other’s score to the maximum cooperative value
claims.source_title: Press & Dyson 2012 PNAS (Discussion)
claims.notes: Also: 'Unlike naive PD, there is no advantage in defection'. Shows the authors themselves framed extortion as a game between 'sentient' players, not as an evolutionary winner.

claims.claim: Press described the discovery as an accident: his program (searching for evolutionarily stable points) kept crashing, which led to ZD strategies; the computer found instances and Dyson generalized them.
claims.quote: The computer could find instances, but not generalize them.
claims.source_title: Edge.org: On 'Iterated Prisoner's Dilemma contains strategies that dominate any evolutionary opponent' (Poundstone, Press, Dyson, Sigmund & Nowak)
claims.notes: Edge page dated 2012-06-18. Press's own reply text. Attribution of 'Dyson did the proof' is my inference from context, not verbatim.

claims.claim: Edge.org's popular framing (William Poundstone) presented Press–Dyson as overturning Axelrod's moral: Axelrod said 'Don't be too clever, don't be unfair'; Press and Dyson supposedly showed cleverness and unfairness triumph.
claims.quote: Press and Dyson have shown that cleverness and unfairness triumph after all.
claims.source_title: Edge.org conversation, Poundstone commentary
claims.notes: Main example of overstatement: generalizes a 1-vs-1 fixed-strategy result to Axelrod's tournament/evolution context.

claims.claim: Dyson himself, on Edge, was skeptical of IPD as a model for evolution of cooperation and summarized Stewart–Plotkin's tournament as 'the strategy that is best for outcome is worst for evolution, and vice versa'.
claims.quote: So the strategy that is best for outcome is worst for evolution, and vice versa.
claims.source_title: Edge.org, Freeman Dyson reply to Stewart & Plotkin
claims.notes: Also verbatim: 'still very skeptical about its use as a model for the evolution of cooperation' and 'Cooperation loses and defection wins.' Context of the latter not fully read — check before quoting it, it may be about a specific scenario.

claims.claim: Sigmund & Nowak (Edge Reality Club, 2012) replied that strategies fixing the opponent's payoff were already known (citing their 1997 'Equal pay for all prisoners'), and that evolution acts at population level, where mutual extortion is self-defeating; the only non-self-defeating norm leads back to Tit-for-Tat.
claims.quote: But biological or cultural evolution is not a phenomenon on the level of the individual.
claims.source_title: Edge.org Reality Club: Karl Sigmund & Martin Nowak
claims.notes: Also verbatim: 'We had known about strategies that allow to nail down the opponent's payoff'. The 1997 paper is Boerlijst, Nowak & Sigmund, 'Equal pay for all prisoners', Am. Math. Monthly 104 (equalizer strategies) — citation detail not separately verified.

claims.claim: MIT Technology Review (2012-08-16) headlined 'The Emerging Revolution in Game Theory', claiming the discovery of 'a winning strategy' for the PD was forcing game theorists to rethink the discipline — while reporting in the same piece Adami & Hintze's finding that ZD strategies are not evolutionarily stable.
claims.quote: The world of game theory is currently on fire.
claims.source_title: MIT Technology Review (arXiv blog), The Emerging Revolution in Game Theory
claims.notes: Subhead: 'The discovery of a winning strategy for Prisoner's Dilemma is forcing game theorists to rethink their discipline.' Also 'nothing short of revolutionary'. Only quoted sources are Adami & Hintze.

claims.claim: Stewart & Plotkin's companion PNAS commentary (109(26):10134–10135, 2012-06-18) stated Press & Dyson had 'changed the game' and noted extortion works best when opponents do not realize they are being extorted; if both know ZD, each tries to extort, giving low payoffs for both.
claims.quote: What is immediately clear is that, by publishing their results, Press and Dyson have changed the game.
claims.source_title: Stewart & Plotkin, Extortion and cooperation in the Prisoner's Dilemma, PNAS (commentary)
claims.notes: Commentary explicitly left evolutionary fate of extortion as open future research. 'Theory of mind' glossed as 'a player who realizes that her behavior can influence her opponents' strategies'.

claims.claim: Stewart & Plotkin reran an Axelrod-like tournament adding ZD strategies: ZDGTFT-2 (generous ZD, enforces S_X−R = 2(S_Y−R)) got the highest total payoff, above TFT and GTFT; Extort-2 (S_X−P = 2(S_Y−P)) got a lower total payoff but won more head-to-head matches than any strategy except Always Defect.
claims.quote: ZDGTFT-2 received the highest total payoff, higher even than Tit-For-Tat and Generous-Tit-For-Tat, the traditional winners.
claims.source_title: Stewart & Plotkin 2012 PNAS commentary, Fig. 1 caption
claims.notes: Earliest primary source for 'extortion wins pairwise but loses the tournament'. Caption: Extort-2 'received a lower total payoff (because its opponents are not evolving), but it won more head-to-head matches than any other strategy, save Always Defect.' NOT stated in the commentary: number of strategies, rounds, payoff numbers, noise. Knight et al. 2024 describe a 19-strategy reproduction 'from Stewart and Plotkin' (secondhand).

claims.claim: Stewart & Plotkin 2013 (PNAS 110(38):15348–15353) found extortion strategies are not successful in evolving populations unless the population is very small; instead 'generous ZD' strategies are evolutionarily robust for all but the smallest population sizes, and all robust strategies are generous.
claims.quote: Extortion strategies are not successful in evolving populations unless the population size is very small.
claims.source_title: Stewart & Plotkin, From extortion to generosity, evolution in the Iterated Prisoner's Dilemma, PNAS
claims.notes: 'Robust' = cannot be selectively replaced by a mutant in a finite population (reduces to ESS as N→∞). Setup: pairwise-comparison/imitation process, weak mutation (monomorphic population), selection strength σ. No numeric N threshold given in text. Generous = after deviation from mutual cooperation, own payoff falls more than opponent's (κ=R condition not text-verified, images). arXiv 1304.7205.

claims.claim: Stewart & Plotkin 2013: WSLS is 'good' but not robust; generous ZD strategies outperform WSLS in some regimes when evolution runs over the full space of memory-one strategies.
claims.source_title: Stewart & Plotkin 2013 (arXiv version)
claims.notes: 'in some regimes' is the qualifier — do not write 'generous ZD beats WSLS'. Paper sometimes misspells WSLS as 'win-lose-stay-shift'.

claims.claim: Adami & Hintze 2013 (Nature Communications 4:2193, published 2013-08-01; preprint arXiv 1208.2666 'Winning isn't everything', Aug 2012) showed ZD strategies (both opponent-score-fixing and extortionate) are at most weakly dominant, not evolutionarily stable, are easily outcompeted by common strategies, and quickly evolve into non-ZD strategies.
claims.quote: Here we show that Zero Determinant strategies are at most weakly dominant, are not evolutionarily stable
claims.source_title: Adami & Hintze, Evolutionary instability of zero-determinant strategies demonstrates that winning is not everything, Nat. Commun.
claims.notes: Quote from arXiv abstract; published abstract has near-identical wording (PMC3741637). Payoffs (R,S,T,P)=(3,0,5,1). Published correction 2014-06-16 (content of correction not checked).

claims.claim: Adami & Hintze: ZD wins every direct competition with Pavlov (WSLS), yet Pavlov is the ESS because it cooperates with itself; replicator dynamics show Pavlov drives ZD extinct regardless of initial density.
claims.quote: Yet, Pavlov is the ESS because it cooperates with itself
claims.source_title: Adami & Hintze 2013 Nat. Commun.
claims.notes: Also verbatim: 'ZD strategies win every single matchup against non-ZD strategies' (Discussion) and 'Thus, ZD wins every direct competition with Pavlov.' Agent-based runs: well-mixed population of 1,024, death-birth/fitness-proportional, 0.1% replacement per update, 1% per-locus mutation; with mutation the population evolves to a stochastic 'general cooperator' (GC). The ZD used is a specific Press–Dyson example — check which p-vector.

claims.claim: Adami & Hintze: ZD can be evolutionarily stable only with an informational advantage — a tag-based ZD ('ZDt') that cooperates with itself and plays ZD against others is favored only if it is the only strategy that can recognize itself; such an advantage is bound to be short-lived.
claims.quote: such an advantage is bound to be short-lived as opposing strategies evolve to counteract the recognition.
claims.source_title: Adami & Hintze 2013 (arXiv/Nat. Commun.)
claims.notes: Note the direction: it is ZD recognizing ZD (self-recognition), not opponents recognizing ZD. The brief's phrasing 'ZD can be beaten if opponents recognize them' is not the paper's claim; the paper says opponents can counter by imitating tags or evolving longer memory.

claims.claim: Hilbe, Nowak & Sigmund 2013 (PNAS 110(17):6913–6918): in reasonably large populations extortioners act as catalysts for cooperation (like TFT) but are not the stable outcome of selection; in very small populations relative payoff differences matter and extortioners hold their ground; in two-population coevolution extortion benefits the slower-evolving population (Red King effect).
claims.quote: they can act as catalysts for the evolution of cooperation, similar to tit-for-tat
claims.source_title: Hilbe, Nowak & Sigmund, Evolution of extortion in Iterated Prisoner's Dilemma games (arXiv 1212.1067)
claims.notes: Quote from preprint; final PNAS abstract wording not retrieved. Small-population threshold is parameter-specific: 'with our parameter values, for M>10' extortion no longer succeeds (donation game b=3, c=1); WSLS beats extortioners in direct contest when M > 1+χ. Extortion defined only for χ>1.

claims.claim: Hilbe, Röhl & Milinski 2014 (Nature Communications 5:3976, 2014-05-29), 'Extortion subdues human players but is finally punished in the prisoner's dilemma': computer ZD strategies vs humans; extortioners beat each human opponent but earned lower payoffs than generous ZD strategies.
claims.quote: Although extortioners succeeded against each of their human opponents, extortion resulted in lower payoffs than generosity.
claims.source_title: Hilbe, Röhl & Milinski, Extortion subdues human players but is finally punished in the prisoner's dilemma, Nat. Commun.
claims.notes: Correct title is '...but is finally punished...', NOT '...outperformed in groups'. No group treatment: all games 1 human vs 1 computer. 60 first-year biology students, 60 rounds (length not announced), subjects not told opponent was a computer. Four ZD treatments by slope s: strong/mild extortion (s=1/3, 2/3), mild/strong generosity (s=2/3, 1/3). Payoffs T=€0.50, R=€0.30, P=€0.10, S=€0. Pooled generosity >18% more payoff (P=0.011).

claims.claim: In Hilbe et al. 2014, humans cooperated 34.2% vs extortioners and 67.7% vs generous ZD; withholding cooperation acted as costly punishment — in the last 10 rounds about a third of humans refused to cooperate with extortioners vs 1 of 30 against generous strategies.
claims.source_title: Hilbe, Röhl & Milinski 2014 Nat. Commun.
claims.notes: Numbers from fetch summary of results section; cooperation vs generous rose 53.0%→76.0% (first vs last 10 rounds), vs extortion 30.3%→39.7% (n.s.). Humans still scored LESS than the extortioner in each pair; the 'punishment' lowers the extortioner's absolute payoff, not below the human's.

claims.claim: Wang, Zhou, Lien, Zheng & Xu 2016 (Nature Communications 7:11125, 2016-04-12): extortion outperformed generosity only when the game was long (500 rounds) and subjects knew the opponent was a computer; with 60 rounds no significant difference; when unaware, generosity scored higher (replicating Hilbe et al.).
claims.quote: More than half of extortionate strategists finally obtain an average score higher than that from mutual cooperation.
claims.source_title: Wang et al., Extortion can outperform generosity in the iterated prisoner's dilemma, Nat. Commun.
claims.notes: 8 treatments (500/60 rounds × aware/unaware × extort/generous), 256 students, 32 per treatment; payoffs 5/3/1/0. In 500A: extortion 2.943 vs generous 2.263 points/round. Intro: 'To our knowledge, this is the first experimental evidence which supports the predictions of the Press–Dyson theory.' Author order per PMC: Zhijian Wang first; Hilbe–Chatterjee–Nowak 2018 ref list cites it as 'Xu, B., Zhou, Y., Lien, J. W., Zheng, J. & Wang, Z.' — discrepancy, use PMC order. Paper does not measure punishment.

claims.claim: Hilbe, Chatterjee & Nowak 2018 review (Nature Human Behaviour 2:469–477): Press & Dyson asked whether Alice can win every pairwise encounter regardless of Bob's strategy and make full cooperation optimal for Bob — answer yes; but evolving populations typically do not settle at extortion; extortioners act as catalysts because they never lose direct competitions and can drift into ALLD populations, then give rise to more cooperative strategies.
claims.quote: Evolving populations, however, typically do not settle at extortion
claims.source_title: Hilbe, Chatterjee & Nowak, Partners and rivals in direct reciprocity, Nat. Hum. Behav.
claims.notes: Author-manuscript PDF. 'Twice the payoff' example requires payoffs rescaled so mutual defection = 0. Also verbatim: 'Evolution leads from extortion to generosity'.

claims.claim: Hilbe–Chatterjee–Nowak 2018: successful strategies are partners (TFT, GTFT, WSLS, Grim — under high continuation probability and sizable benefit) or rivals (ALLD, extortioners); small populations and few rounds favor rivalry, large populations and stable relationships favor partners; only in infinitely repeated undiscounted games is TFT both partner and rival.
claims.quote: Whereas small population sizes and a limited number of rounds favor rivalry, partner strategies are selected when populations are large and relationships stable.
claims.source_title: Hilbe, Chatterjee & Nowak 2018 Nat. Hum. Behav. (abstract)
claims.notes: TFT dual status: 'it does not lose out in any pairwise encounter, while still making sure that it yields the mutual cooperation payoff against players of the same kind.' Same review restates Axelrod: TFT 'did not win any pairwise encounter' yet had highest average score — the mirror image of extortion.

claims.claim: Hilbe–Chatterjee–Nowak 2018 summarize the human experiments: extortioner beat each human in direct encounter but generous program earned higher average payoffs; fairness concerns explain this, and they vanished when participants were told they faced a computer program. They also note extortion can succeed via chosen representatives (Milinski et al. 2016 Nat. Commun. 7:10915, climate game) and power asymmetry (Hilbe, Hagel & Milinski, PLoS ONE).
claims.quote: While the extortionate program indeed outperformed each human opponent in the direct encounter, it was the generous program that reached on average higher payoffs than the extortioner.
claims.source_title: Hilbe, Chatterjee & Nowak 2018 Nat. Hum. Behav.
claims.notes: Secondhand summary of primary experiments. Review says subjects 'did not obtain any information about the nature of their opponent' — true for Hilbe 2014 and the unaware arms of Wang 2016 only. Milinski 2016 and Hilbe-Hagel-Milinski primary papers NOT fetched.

claims.claim: Hilbe, Traulsen & Sigmund 2015 (Games and Economic Behavior 92:41–52) 'Partners or rivals?' characterize within memory-one strategies: partner strategies (fair share of social optimum, unfair co-player penalized), competitive strategies (never less than co-player) and ZD strategies (enforce linear payoff relation), properties holding against any co-player strategy, memory-one or not.
claims.source_title: Hilbe, Traulsen & Sigmund, Partners or rivals? Strategies for the iterated prisoner's dilemma, GEB
claims.notes: Venue is Games and Economic Behavior, not the journal 'Games'. Abstract content from search snippets, full text not fetched.

claims.claim: Knight, Harper, Glynatsi & Gillard (PLoS ONE 19(7):e0304641, 2024; arXiv 1904.00973, 2019): in large Axelrod-library tournaments (204 strategies), extortionate strategies achieve many wins but generally not a high score and fail to be evolutionarily stable; top scorers are 'selectively extortionate' (extort weak opponents, cooperate with strong ones), and ZD strategies can be outperformed by non-ZD strategies.
claims.quote: Extortionate strategies achieve a high number of wins but they do generally not achieve a high score
claims.source_title: Knight et al., Recognising and evaluating the effectiveness of extortion in the Iterated Prisoner's Dilemma, PLoS ONE
claims.notes: Best modern source for 'ZD wins every pairwise match but loses tournaments' (plus Stewart–Plotkin 2012 Fig.1 and Adami–Hintze 2013). Also 'Infamously, extortionate strategies do not play well with themselves.' Results depend on strategy pool; no noise/fixed lengths in parts of design.

claims.claim: Quanta Magazine (Emily Singer, 2015-02-12) framed Press–Dyson as suggesting 'the best strategies were selfish ones that led to extortion, not cooperation', then reported Stewart–Plotkin's finding that generous strategies were most successful in evolving populations.
claims.quote: It suggested the best strategies were selfish ones that led to extortion, not cooperation.
claims.source_title: Quanta Magazine, Game Theory Calls Cooperation Into Question
claims.notes: Plotkin quoted: 'The most robust strategies, the ones that can't be replaced by other strategies, are generous.' The Plotkin 'defection rules the day' quote refers to later work (Stewart & Plotkin 2014, coevolving payoffs) — do not attach it to ZD. Republished in Scientific American.

open_questions: Exact full abstract of Press & Dyson 2012 not transcribed (tool quote limit); copy from PMC3387070 directly. PNAS doi page 403.
Press–Dyson χ parameterization and the precise limit giving TFT are in equation images; verify in PDF that TFT corresponds to χ=1 (and the 13/3 limiting score mentioned in the text).
Stewart & Plotkin 2012 tournament parameters (number of strategies, rounds, payoffs) not stated in commentary; possibly in SI. Knight et al. say a 19-strategy reproduction.
No 'Nature news' piece on Press–Dyson located; may not exist or may be under a different title. Unverified.
Dyson's IAS Letter (Fall 2012) piece returned 403 — not read.
Hilbe–Nowak–Sigmund 2013 final PNAS abstract wording not checked (preprint used).

No paper titled 'Extortion subdues human players but is outperformed in groups' exists as far as found; the correct title ends 'but is finally punished in the prisoner's dilemma'. Possible confusion with Hilbe, Wu, Traulsen & Nowak 2014 PNAS 'Cooperation and control in multiplayer social dilemmas' (extortion in groups) — not fetched.
Milinski et al. 2016 (representatives) and Hilbe–Hagel–Milinski (asymmetric power) primary papers not fetched; Becks & Milinski 2019 not checked.
Author order discrepancy for Nat. Commun. 7:11125 (PMC: Wang first; HCN 2018 ref list: Xu first).
